title: Work inequality is organized through sector, formality, own-account status, and circumstances beyond individual control rather than only headline wage gaps
source_unit: International Labour Organization, Inequalities in the World of Work, published June 2026
geography: Global labor markets with comparative analysis across Sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, demographic groups, sectors, employment forms, and formal/informal work

denominator.unit: ILO harmonized labor-market evidence and global inequality-analysis frame

inequality_dimensions.value: vertical inequality, horizontal disparities, and inequality of opportunity

horizontal_measures.value: differences across demographic and labour-market groups

opportunity_mechanism.value: circumstances beyond individual control account for a measurable share of wage dispersion

observations.method: ILO multidimensional analysis using harmonized ILO microdata, relative and absolute earnings measures, group comparisons, and decomposition of inequality of opportunity.
observations.uncertainty: The publication is a comparative synthesis of harmonized data and decompositions; it does not establish a universal causal effect of any single circumstance, sector, or policy on an individual's earnings.
observations.subgroup: Workers across demographic groups, sectors, employment forms, formal and informal economies, own-account work, employers, and labor institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Observed earnings inequality can reflect skill, experience, occupation, hours, geography, selection, firm composition, or compensation differences as well as structural barriers; no single decomposition captures the whole mechanism.

observations.period: 2026 publication; sectoral, regional, and employment-form inequality

denominator.unit: global earnings-inequality comparison across regions and work forms

high_inequality_regions.value: Sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America consistently exhibit high earnings inequality

absolute_gap_signal.value: absolute earnings measures reveal particularly wide material gaps

sector_formality_role.value: sectoral differences and employment form account for a large role in inequality of opportunity

own_account_within_group.value: own-account workers show substantial within-group earnings inequality, especially in the informal economy

observations.method: ILO regional, sectoral, and employment-form comparisons using harmonized earnings data and decomposition results.
observations.uncertainty: Regional and work-form patterns do not identify all country-specific mechanisms, earnings trajectories, working conditions, or household consequences; harmonization and coverage vary across sources.
observations.subgroup: Informal workers, own-account workers, employees, women and men, workers in different sectors, and labor markets in Sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America.
observations.counterinterpretation: Own-account work can offer autonomy and entry when wage employment is scarce; informal activity can provide income and flexibility even while exposing workers to weaker protection and greater volatility.

observations.period: 2026; policy and institutional implications for decent work

denominator.unit: ILO work-inequality policy and labor-market segmentation frame

structural_policy_set.value: comprehensive labor-market policies, formal-employment expansion, and improved access to decent work

segmentation_endpoint.value: sectoral segmentation and employment form shape access to earnings and protections

gender_intersection.value: sex contributes less to between-group inequality in the decomposition but remains important when intersecting disadvantages are considered

decent_work_endpoint.value: earnings, formality, opportunity, and protection must be considered together to assess inclusive work

observations.method: ILO interpretation of decomposition results and policy implications for formalization, decent work, labor-market segmentation, and intersecting disadvantage.
observations.uncertainty: Policy priorities are not implementation evaluations; formalization alone does not guarantee adequate earnings, bargaining power, safety, flexibility, or household recovery.
observations.subgroup: Workers in informal and formal employment, own-account workers, employers, labor ministries, social-protection institutions, and worker organizations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some formalization policies can exclude marginal workers or reduce flexible earning routes if they raise compliance costs without support; policy should distinguish protection from employment status alone.

related_sources.claim: Official ILO DOI for Inequalities in the World of Work.
ILO Employment and Social Trends 2026 provides a separate global jobs-gap and job-quality context; it is not treated as the same inequality mechanism here.

boundary: This record adds a published structural work-inequality route linking earnings dispersion, sector, formality, own-account work, inequality of opportunity, policy, and decent-work access. It is not new respondent-level analysis, an individual wage estimate, a causal decomposition for every country, or proof that formalization or policy reform improves household outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official ILO publication page and DOI metadata were reviewed; multidimensional inequality, regional and employment-form patterns, inequality-of-opportunity decomposition, intersectional interpretation, and policy boundaries were cross-checked.
